chapter: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
title: Recording in Chicago at Bill Putnam's studio; friendly rivalry with Fletcher
summary: Horace's Okeh and Decca records came after the 5100 Club, cut at Bill Putnam's Chicago studio where Fletcher also recorded; the brothers ran friendly opposition on the air.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So they did know the band because of the broadcasts. What about recording? Were you doing much recording? Now, we're still talking about this Swingland time, 1937.

I think we had just begun on the tail end of that for recording. This is when I made this 'Ginger Bell' and things, you know. Because we had moved on from Swingland -- if I'm not ahead of myself -- (unintelligible) to the 5100 Club.
I have that -- let's see, you went at the Savoy in Chicago.
And then also Grand Terrace in 1939 and later the 5100 Club.
Later the 5100 Club, because this is where we were more or less discovered by the recording studio.
There was a guy that had a recording studio in Chicago. He had excellent equipment, named Bill Putnam. Remember him?

(Inaudible) In fact, the bands from all over used to come to Chicago to record there out on Ontario on the north side. And this is where I made my OKeh and Decca recordings. Fletcher also recorded, if I remember correctly, in this particular studio, too.
During this time, again late thirties, Fletcher was in Chicago some of that time, wasn't he? At the Grand Terrace?
Yes. In fact, we used to run opposition to each other, you know? Even on the air, he used to broadcast too, you know.
Did you actually feel any opposition? I mean, other than just sort of friendly rivalry or --
